title: Should Wisdom Be the Goal of Schools?
author: Lead Time Blog
summary: Prompted by the observation that every technological revolution changes what is scarce, this piece argues that AI's commodification of intelligence should prompt schools to reorient their goals from knowledge acquisition toward wisdom. The author frames wisdom as having three components: knowledge (the engine), agency (the driver), and wisdom itself (the judge of where action should go). Knowledge remains essential — the science of learning confirms that expertise depends on richly organized long-term memory — but it is the destination that needs updating. Agency develops when decisions carry real consequences, not when students are told to be resilient. Wisdom is described not as a fixed personality trait but as what richly organized knowledge refined through experience looks like when applied to complex problems. The Lindy Effect is proposed as a curriculum filter: favor knowledge that has endured because enduring principles are more likely to transfer across domains than generic skills.
points: Every technological revolution changes what is scarce: the printing press made literacy valuable, the internet made interpretation valuable, and AI appears to be commodifying intelligence itself — shifting the premium toward wisdom.
Knowledge remains the non-negotiable foundation: the science of learning shows that thinking depends on knowledge, and AI doesn't change this — it makes it more important, not less.

Agency — the capacity to act intentionally, own decisions and their consequences, and influence the world toward worthwhile goals — is what schools must build alongside knowledge; AI can optimize means but cannot determine worthwhile ends.

Wisdom is not a fixed personality trait but an emergent property of well-organized knowledge refined by experience and reflection — essentially what knowledge-anchored transfer looks like at its highest level.

The Lindy Effect offers a useful curriculum filter: favor ideas that have survived centuries (opportunity cost, Stoic agency, constitutional government, Euclidean geometry) because enduring principles transfer more reliably than generic skills.
quotes: The internet made information abundant. Knowing where to find it became less valuable than knowing what to trust.
they all start from the same assumption: that the purpose of schooling should be defined by AI’s current capabilities.
The science of learning hasn’t changed because AI exists. Human memory still builds knowledge. Expertise still depends on richly organised long-term memory. Judgement still depends on what we know.
AI may make access to intelligence cheaper, but it cannot shortcut the knowledge humans need to think well.
AI can optimise means, but it cannot determine worthwhile ends. It can generate answers but cannot care whether they are acted upon.
Knowledge remains the engine. Agency puts it to work. Wisdom decides where it should go.
